analysis.one_liner: Lets consumer-product safety regulators issue safety standards for firearms for the first time.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate Commerce Committee on May 4, 2023, and no further action was taken before Congress ended on January 3, 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: Federal consumer product safety law explicitly excludes firearms, so the agency that can order a recall of a defective space heater cannot do the same for a defective gun. This bill would delete that exclusion, letting the Consumer Product Safety Commission write safety standards for guns and their components. The bill was referred to the Senate Commerce Committee and never received a hearing, a vote, or any further action before the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: If it passed, the benefit would flow to anyone exposed to defective or poorly designed firearms — households with guns, people near gun violence, and communities affected by firearm deaths — since a federal agency could for the first time require design changes, recalls, and safety testing for guns and their components [S2][S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Households and communities exposed to firearms

how_it_helps.text: The bill removes the statutory carve-out that keeps pistols, revolvers, and other firearms outside the Consumer Product Safety Commission's jurisdiction, allowing the agency to issue safety standards for guns and firearm components [S2][S3].

This would subject firearms to the same kind of independent federal review for defects and safety hazards that applies to other consumer goods, something gun manufacturers have been statutorily shielded from since 1976 [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Firearm manufacturers would bear the cost of meeting federal safety standards, testing, and potential recalls for design defects [S2][S3]. Some of that cost could be passed to buyers through higher prices.
analysis.who_pays_short: Gun manufacturers, possibly buyers via prices

drawbacks.text: The bill only permits the Commission to act; it does not itself set standards, so the real-world benefit depends on future agency rulemaking that could be slow, narrow, or unwritten.

Opponents of CPSC authority over firearms argue that safety standards could raise manufacturing costs or effectively restrict certain gun designs, treating a long-standing statutory exemption for firearms as a deliberate boundary on federal regulation of guns.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit — subjecting firearms to the same independent safety review as toys, space heaters, and power tools — is real but incremental: it addresses design and safety defects, not who can buy a gun. The cost, in the view of opponents, is expanding federal authority over firearms manufacturing in ways that could raise prices or restrict designs; the industry has long operated free of product-safety rules by statute. On the merits it is a modest, targeted regulatory change whose practical effect depends entirely on what standards the Commission later adopts.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate bill was read twice and sent to the Commerce Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never acted on it before the 118th Congress ended, so it died.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on May 4, 2023, and the same day was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation [S5][S1].
The committee never held a markup or reported the bill, and no further action appears in the record; the 118th Congress ended January 3, 2025, killing the bill [S5][S1].
All eight cosponsors were Democrats, and no Republican signed on, so the bill had no clear path in a Senate where most legislation requires some bipartisan support [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Firearm manufacturers keep their decades-old exemption from consumer product safety regulation, and no federal safety standards can apply to guns as a result. The 3,000+ people who sponsored or cosponsored it wanted a change, but the outcome preserves the status quo for the industry.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Gun makers, who kept their regulatory exemption

industries.note: The bill would strip gun makers of a decades-old statutory exemption from federal product-safety oversight, exposing them to safety standards and potential recalls for defects. Their interest ran against the bill, which died in committee before any rules could be proposed.

industries.industry: Consumer Product Safety Commission (as an institution)
industries.note: The bill would expand the agency's jurisdiction to cover firearms for the first time. Because the bill never advanced, the agency's role stayed unchanged.
